When powered, it detects pressure via sensors and provides vibration feedback through a haptic motor. The feel depends entirely on the manufacturer's tuning. Full‑area mechanical touchpad: the entire surface clicks down (unlike traditional touchpads where only the bottom half moves). However, on many Windows laptops, the required force differs between the top and bottom areas. Strongly recommended: go to an Apple store and try the MacBook Pro's haptic touchpad (the industry benchmark for haptic feedback) and the MacBook Neo's full‑area mechanical touchpad (the benchmark for that type). Get a feel for their uniform, responsive clicks. Then come back and try Windows counterparts – you will immediately know what level of quality you can accept. 1.4 Laptop Classifications Thin and light: portable, long battery life, quiet. Uses low‑power CPU, no discrete GPU. Thickness around 15mm, weight under 1.3kg. Suitable for office work, study, light entertainment. Gaming laptop: high performance, with a high‑power CPU and mid‑range to high‑end discrete GPU. Heavy cooling, weight often exceeds 2kg. Suitable for demanding games, professional video editing, etc. All‑rounder / creator laptop: sits between the two – somewhat portable (around 1.8kg), with an entry‑level or mid‑range discrete GPU. Can handle office work and light gaming. 1.5 Buying Reference: 笔吧评测室 笔吧评测室 is one of the more authoritative laptop review sources in China. Follow their WeChat public account or Bilibili channel (also on Douyin and Xiaohongshu). Their WeChat account publishes weekly curated recommendations by price range, with detailed explanations. Read those to narrow down a few candidate models, then search for in‑depth reviews and user feedback. 1.6 Purchase Advice (2026) Prices are high: laptop prices are at historical highs in 2026. If you are not in urgent need (e.g., your current computer still works), you can wait – prices will likely drop. If you must buy: thin‑and‑light laptops offer better value in the current market. The iGPU performance of modern high‑end thin‑and‑light laptops is sufficient for many games and daily software. Government subsidies: many provinces offer 10‑20% consumer subsidies. If possible, consider travelling to a province with such subsidies to buy your laptop. Search for "province name + appliance subsidy" for details. 1.7 From Unboxing to Activation: Inspection Procedure (Core Steps) When you receive your laptop, follow these steps. Before activation, you have unconditional return rights. If you find any problem, return it immediately – do not attempt to fix it yourself. Check the packaging and exterior Confirm that the seals are intact. Inspect the lid (A‑cover) and bottom (D‑cover) for scratches or dents. Check the power adapter and charging port for signs of use. Gently open and close the lid a few times; listen for creaking. For a mechanical (traditional hinged) touchpad: gently wiggle the edges to see if it rocks, and press all four corners to feel for consistent resistance. For a haptic touchpad: test the feedback in different areas after booting into the OS. Lightly press different areas of the keyboard to feel for overall rigidity. If you find any anomaly that you couldn't accept, take photos at once and contact customer service for a return. Transport mode test Do not plug in the power adapter. Press the power button once. If it does not turn on → normal, proceed. If it turns on and boots into the OS immediately → the unit has been used. Return it immediately. First boot setup (skip internet) When you reach the login screen, do not connect to Wi‑Fi. To bypass Windows 11's forced internet requirement: At the region selection screen, press to open Command Prompt. Type and press Enter. The system will restart. After reboot, when you reach the "Let's connect you to a network" screen, click "I don't have internet" → "Continue with limited setup". Log in with a local account (use an English alphanumeric username). Screen inspection After entering the desktop, right‑click → Personalize → Background → Choose a solid color. Cycle through pure white, pure black, pure red, pure green, and pure blue. Carefully look for dead pixels (unexpected bright or dark dots). On a pure black background, check for backlight bleed. Minor IPS glow at the edges is normal, but if a corner glows like a small flashlight, consider a return. Verify the configuration Press Win + X → Task Manager → Performance to confirm CPU model and RAM capacity. Download a drive inspection tool (e.g., CrystalDiskInfo) to check the SSD's brand and model against reviews. CrystalDiskInfo's Offical Download Site: Or you may download with Usability test Lift the laptop with one hand – any unusual creaking? Plug in a USB drive and a mouse; confirm all ports work. After fully charging, use it on battery for an hour of light use to rule out abnormal battery drain. 7‑day no‑questions‑asked return If you find any of the following: dead pixels (especially in the centre), backlight bleed affecting normal viewing, abnormal touchpad click feel, unusual battery wear, or widespread reports of a defect in this batch – directly request a return (not an exchange) and either reorder or switch to another brand. Create a Microsoft account and activate Go to signup.live.com and create a free account. Log in to activate the pre‑installed Office suite (within 30 days, otherwise the license may expire). With an account, you can digitally reactivate Windows after a clean reinstall without entering a product key. Finally, connect to the internet After all checks are complete, connect to Wi‑Fi. Windows and Office will activate automatically. Extended Reading The following sections contain detailed technical discussions and advanced knowledge. Each is independent – you can read any of them without relying on the must‑read part. Extended 1: CPU Models and Performance Mainstream thin‑and‑light laptops in 2026 use CPUs such as the Intel Core Ultra 5 338H、Ultra X7 358H、Ultra X9 388H. Mainstream gaming laptops often pair an Intel Ultra 7 356H with an NVIDIA RTX 5060 or 5070. Laptop CPU naming can be confusing – the same architecture may spawn multiple model numbers. For example, AMD's 8845H is essentially a rebranded 7845H (identical specifications, only the name differs). Always search for performance reviews of the exact model before buying; do not judge by the numbers alone. Extended 2: iGPU Gaming – Expectations vs. Reality Some marketing claims "iGPU performance close to an RTX 3050 Ti". However, note that an iGPU has no dedicated video memory – it borrows system RAM – and the CPU and iGPU share the same thermal solution. Under sustained gaming loads, the CPU and iGPU compete for power and thermal headroom, so real‑world performance often falls short of benchmark numbers. If you plan to play AAA games on an iGPU laptop, watch game‑specific tests by reviewers like 笔吧评测室 before deciding. Extended 3: Sleep States (S0ix vs. S3) Windows defines several power sleep states. S3, known as "Suspend to RAM", powers down the CPU and most hardware while keeping RAM refreshed – wake‑up is very fast (about 1‑2 seconds). S0ix (Modern Standby, also called S2idle) is a low‑power idle state promoted by Microsoft since Windows 8, allowing the system to stay connected and update while the screen is off – similar to a smartphone. However, it can cause heat, battery drain, and unreliable wake‑up. Since Intel Meteor Lake (12th‑gen Core), Microsoft has required hardware vendors to drop full support for S3. Consequently, many new laptops support only S0ix. Even running Linux, the ACPI tables are stripped of S3 code, making reliable sleep impossible. If sleep reliability matters to you, check community feedback before buying – some business laptops (e.g., certain ThinkPad models) still retain S3 options. Extended 4: Touchpad Tuning Differences Even among haptic touchpads, the vibration feedback varies greatly by manufacturer – for example, Xiaomi and Honor feel completely different. Therefore, it is worth visiting a physical store to try them yourself. If you are unsure what you like, first try the MacBook Pro's haptic touchpad (the industry benchmark) and the MacBook Neo's full‑area mechanical touchpad (also a benchmark). Then compare with Windows laptops – you will clearly see what level of quality you can accept. Extended 5: Storage Drive Selection NAND Manufacturers vs. Assembly Houses The core of an SSD is the NAND flash chip. Companies that manufacture their own NAND are called NAND manufacturers or IDMs. Major active NAND manufacturers include Samsung, SK hynix (including the acquired Intel NAND business, now Solidigm), Micron, Kioxia, Western Digital, and China's YMTC. YMTC's Xtacking architecture (e.g., X4‑9040) is competitive in both performance and cost. The controller is the "small CPU" of an SSD, handling data management, wear leveling, garbage collection, etc. Notable retail controller vendors include Silicon Motion, Phison, Maxio, and InnoGrit. TLC vs. QLC TLC (Triple‑Level Cell): stores 3 bits per cell – good write endurance and speed. QLC (Quad‑Level Cell): stores 4 bits per cell – higher density, lower cost, but significantly worse write endurance and write speed. For a system drive or frequent large writes, QLC is generally not recommended. The Solidigm P41 Plus is a rare exception – its excellent firmware mitigates QLC's drawbacks. Original vs. Third‑party SSDs Original SSD: designed, packaged, and sold by the NAND manufacturer itself – e.g., Samsung, Western Digital, Kioxia, ZhiTai. Third‑party SSD: buys raw NAND wafers and then packages, tests, and assembles them – e.g., Kingston, ADATA. Quality depends on the vendor's packaging capability. Vendors with their own packaging and rigorous testing (e.g., UMIS's UnionMemory brand) are acceptable. Avoid any brand that only does sticker assembly – their NAND sources are unknown, and the drive may fail at any moment. OEM vs. Retail Drives OEM and retail drives are identical hardware. Retail drives come with official warranty and driver support; OEM drives are warrantied through the channel vendor at a lower price. OEM drives are typically sourced through secondary channels – always verify the seller's warranty terms before purchase. Personal Recommendations (for reference only) My first recommendation is original SSDs, e.g., ZhiTai TiPro 9000. Among OEM drives, the following three are worth considering: PVC10 (SK hynix) PCB01 (SK hynix) AM6C1 (UnionMemory, under UMIS) Avoid Samsung PM9A1 and any model known for "0e" errors (uncorrectable data corruption leading to permanent data loss). Also avoid any white‑label, gray‑label, or no‑name SSDs. Your storage drive holds all your important data – essays, photos, code, game saves. A low‑quality drive may die suddenly, and data recovery is expensive and not guaranteed. Saving a few dollars is not worth that risk. Considerations for Adding an SSD to a Laptop Before adding an SSD to your laptop, check the following: Empty M.2 slot: search for motherboard photos or disassembly videos of your model. The second slot on some laptops may only support short drives (2242 or 2230); installing a 2280 drive may not fit. M.2 form factors: common lengths are 2230 (30mm), 2242 (42mm), and 2280 (80mm). 2280 is the most common. For 2242, the PVC10 and PC411 are worthwhile choices. Power consumption and drop‑out risk: laptops have far less power delivery and cooling than desktops. Verify the drive's sustained power consumption – a high‑power drive can overheat and disconnect in a thin‑and‑light. Recommended reviewers: Bilibili creators "前进的四火" and "HOMOLAB" produce high‑quality SSD reviews – they use professional tools like fio for steady‑state testing, not just peak speeds. Current timing: SSD prices are high in 2026 – if not urgent, wait for prices to drop. Extended 6: Display Selection Display preference is subjective – I strongly recommend visiting a physical store to compare different panels with your own eyes. Personal preference Some users prefer high‑quality LCD panels (especially IPS or MiniLED backlit) because LCD has no OLED burn‑in risk, higher full‑screen brightness, and sharper text. Resolution vs. Refresh Rate Compared to high refresh rates (e.g., 120Hz), high resolution (e.g., 2560×1600 or 3840×2160) delivers crisper text and images, significantly improving productivity for office work, coding, and reading. 60Hz is sufficient for non‑competitive gaming. When budget is limited, prioritising resolution is a reasonable choice. Color Accuracy and Gamut Coverage Color accuracy (measured by Delta E) and gamut coverage are equally important. Color accuracy affects your judgement of colours – for example, you take a photo with your phone, edit it in Lightroom on your laptop; if the display is inaccurate, the colours you adjust may look completely wrong to others. Even for casual photo editing or watching movies, you want colours to be reasonably true. Gamut coverage determines how many colours the display can show – common standards include sRGB, DCI‑P3, etc. For most users, covering 100% sRGB is the baseline. Factory Calibration and Calibrators Modern thin‑and‑light laptops generally have decent out‑of‑box colour accuracy, but do not blindly trust "factory calibrated" claims. Factory calibration is often done on a few samples, and the reported Delta E is measured under specific brightness and mode – it does not guarantee your unit is the same. If you truly demand high colour accuracy (note: if you do not know what "colour accuracy" means, you probably do not need it for the foreseeable future), the most reliable method is to rent a colorimeter (e.g., Spyder or Calibrite) and calibrate your screen following a tutorial. Generate and load an ICC profile. Calibrate once a year. Extended 7: Buying Principles for Gaming and All‑rounder Laptops For gaming laptops, a common core principle is: given acceptable performance release and a decent display, choose the cheapest one. Different brands with the same CPU/GPU can have vastly different sustained power limits (i.e., performance release). Check real cooling and stress tests from reviewers like 笔吧评测室. Only after confirming that performance release is not crippled should you compare prices. For all‑rounder laptops, trying them in person is recommended – chassis thickness, cooling, and fan noise vary greatly between models.

title: SystemTuningANDAntimalware
content: Appendix 2: System Tuning and Antimalware This chapter covers only the most essential maintenance principles and operations. More in‑depth discussions are in the "Extended Reading" section that follows. 2.1 Core Principle: If You Don‘t Understand It, Don't Touch It The default configuration of Windows has been thoroughly tested and works well for the vast majority of use cases. Many online "optimisation" guides tell you to disable certain system services to free up memory, but this often breaks features you may need later (e.g., disabling the print spooler makes printers unusable), and you are unlikely to remember that you disabled it. The only safe rule: if you do not know exactly what a setting does, do not change it. Using your computer normally without blindly tweaking settings is the best optimisation. 2.2 Antimalware: The Built‑In One Is Good Enough Windows comes with Microsoft Defender Antimalware, which is more than sufficient for most personal users. Its signatures update frequently, it integrates deeply with the system, and it does not consume excessive resources. For the vast majority of people, no third‑party antimalware is needed. 2.3 Handling Third‑Party Security Software 2.3.1 Chinese Security Suites: Generally Not Needed Software such as 360, Tencent PC Manager, and Kingsoft Antivirus is usually not recommended. They often bring pop‑up ads, bundled promotions, consume background resources, and may even have security vulnerabilities of their own. 2.3.2 Pre‑installed McAfee: Recommended to Uninstall Many branded laptops (e.g., some Asus and Dell models) come with a pre‑installed McAfee trial, often including a two‑year license. Given that McAfee has had security vulnerabilities in the past and runs at the kernel driver level, issues can be serious. It is advisable to uninstall it. Search for "McAfee Consumer Product Removal tool" – run it to cleanly remove everything. 2.4 Manufacturer Pre‑installed Software: Keep Only the Control Centre Branded laptops come with various pre‑installed software. The only thing worth keeping is the hardware control centre, for example: Lenovo Vantage (Lenovo) Armoury Crate (Asus) Dell Power Manager (Dell) These tools let you adjust performance modes, fan speeds, battery charge thresholds, etc. All other pre‑installed software (e.g., AI assistants, music players, app store promotions, trial software) can be safely uninstalled. 2.5 Do Not Fill Up Your C: Drive (The Most Important Optimisation) Keep at least 20% free space on your C: drive (i.e., usage below 80%). If the C: drive runs out of space, your computer will become noticeably slow, because Windows uses the hard drive as temporary memory (swap). Once your C: drive gets close to full, immediately clean up unnecessary files or move your user folders (Documents, Downloads, Desktop, etc.) to another drive. Search online for "how to change the location of user folders in Windows" for instructions. 2.6 Good Habits Are the Best Security Measure Download software only from official websites or the Microsoft Store. Do not click random pop‑up ads, especially those claiming "Your computer is infected". Do not plug in unknown USB drives without caution. When installing any software, do not blindly click "Next" repeatedly. Slow down and check each step for options such as "install XX browser", "set as homepage", or "install to the C: drive" (you may prefer D:). Uncheck any options you do not need. Once you develop these habits, Microsoft Defender will handle the remaining security risks adequately. 2.7 First Steps After You First Boot into the System After connecting to the internet, go to Settings → Windows Update → "Check for updates". Install all available updates (may require several restarts). Go to Settings → Apps, and uninstall unnecessary pre‑installed software (including McAfee). Restart your PC. In the system tray, confirm that the Microsoft Defender shield icon is present and healthy. 2.8 Windows Update: Do Not Disable It Many old tutorials suggest "disabling Windows Update" because it consumes bandwidth or may restart your computer. That advice no longer applies today. Windows Update does far more than just fixing security holes. It also: Automatically updates many Microsoft applications, such as Office suites and runtimes. Updates hardware drivers (graphics, network, audio, etc.), preventing blue screens or performance issues caused by outdated drivers. Updates Windows Defender's virus definitions, keeping your computer protected against the latest threats. If you worry about sudden reboots interrupting your work, do this instead: Go to Settings → Windows Update → Advanced options → Active hours. Set the time period when you normally use your computer (e.g., 09:00 to 18:00). Windows will not automatically restart during those hours. Outside active hours, if a restart is required for an update, Windows will do it when idle, or you can manually choose a restart time. Not updating Windows does NOT make your system more stable. On the contrary, skipping updates for a long time accumulates unpatched vulnerabilities and driver bugs, which may lead to blue screens, sluggishness, or even malware attacks. Leave automatic updates on, configure active hours properly – that is the smarter approach. Extended Reading The following sections contain detailed technical discussions and advanced knowledge. Each is independent – you can read any of them without relying on the must‑read part. Extended 1: Why You Should Not Mess with the Registry and Group Policy The Registry is Windows's configuration database, storing almost every setting for hardware, software, and users. Group Policy is a graphical interface for configuring the Registry in bulk. Incorrect modifications can render the system unbootable or break features permanently. For example, someone disabled the Print Spooler to "save memory", and months later could not print – it took them a long time to realise they had turned it off. If you do not know what these tools are, stay away from them entirely. Extended 2: Microsoft Defender vs. Common Chinese Security Suites Microsoft Defender has no ads, no pop‑ups, does not collect personal usage data, and uses few resources. By contrast, Chinese security suites (e.g., 360, Tencent PC Manager) offer extra gadgets (software updaters, network speed tests) but at the cost of frequent ad pop‑ups, bundled installs, and background data uploads. In major international security tests, Microsoft Defender consistently ranks in the top tier. For non‑high‑risk personal use, Defender is the safer choice. Extended 3: How to Uninstall McAfee Properly McAfee is recommended for removal not only because of past security vulnerabilities (e.g., remote code execution), but also because it is notoriously difficult to uninstall fully – normal "Add/Remove Programs" often leaves behind drivers and services. Use the official "McAfee Consumer Product Removal" from McAfee's website. Run it to automatically detect and clean everything. If your laptop is brand new and you haven't activated McAfee yet, uninstalling from Settings is cleaner and leaves fewer traces. Extended 4: Categorising Manufacturer Pre‑installed Software Must keep: Hardware control centre (performance modes, fans, battery thresholds). Without it, you may lose the ability to adjust screen brightness, keyboard backlight, or set charge limits. Safe to remove: "AI assistants", "PC manager", app store promotions, music/video trials, cloud storage promotions – most are third‑party customisations with mediocre experience and resource usage. Optional: Driver update utilities from the manufacturer (e.g., Lenovo Driver Manager). If you can download drivers from the official website yourself, you can remove these as well. Extended 5: Swap (Virtual Memory) Explained Operating systems use a mechanism called swap (or page file). When physical RAM is insufficient, the system moves some temporarily unused data from RAM to a file on the hard drive (pagefile.sys), freeing RAM for active programs. Even when physical RAM is abundant, Windows may pre‑swap some data to optimise memory layout. This page file resides on the C: drive by default. If the C: drive has very little free space, the page file cannot expand properly, or the free space is fragmented. The system then constantly reads and writes to the hard drive for swapping, making the computer extremely slow. This is why a full C: drive is disastrous. Extended 6: SLC Cache and Write Principles on SSDs Most consumer SSDs use TLC (3 bits per cell) or QLC (4 bits per cell) NAND. To boost write speed, the SSD internally reserves a portion as SLC cache (1 bit per cell, fast writing). When the amount of data written exceeds the cache size, the drive switches to TLC/QLC direct write mode, and speed drops dramatically. When SSD usage exceeds roughly 60%, the controller gradually reduces or even disables the SLC cache, forcing TLC direct write. Worse, the remaining free space is often not a single contiguous area – it is scattered with logical traces of deleted files. Writing new data then requires the SSD to read the existing block, modify it in memory, and write it back (read‑modify‑write). This further reduces performance and increases write amplification, shortening the drive's lifespan. Therefore, keeping your C: drive sufficiently free is not only for virtual memory but also to maintain the SSD's high‑speed writing capability. Extended 7: Malware‑Patch and Similar Tools Malware‑Patch is a small open‑source tool (project page: https://github.com/the1812/Malware-Patch). It does not actively scan for malware; instead, it uses UAC (User Account Control – the pop‑up that asks for permission when installing software) to intercept installation attempts by common unwanted software. When you double‑click on certain "family bucket" installers, it shows a warning. For beginners, this is a mild aid, but it is not essential. If you already have the habit of downloading software only from official sources, you do not need it. Extended 8: On "Make Your PC Fly" Optimisation Videos Many online videos claim that a few registry tweaks can dramatically boost performance. Most such "optimisations" are either placebo, trade stability for a tiny gain, or even disable important security mechanisms. The only real ways to keep a computer running smoothly are: Keep enough free space on your C: drive. Ensure proper cooling (clean dust, elevate the laptop). Do not install software that noticeably slows down the system (e.g., certain antimalware suites). For everything else, Windows manages memory and background processes on its own. Trust the default configuration and spend your time on real work and entertainment – that is the best optimisation. Extended 9: The Myth of "Disabling Windows Update" There was once a popular belief that disabling Windows Update improves performance and avoids forced restarts. This stemmed from the poor update experience and lack of restart control in early Windows versions (like Windows 7/8). Since Windows 10, Microsoft has significantly improved the update mechanism: Most updates download silently in the background, consuming little to no foreground resources. The "Active hours" feature gives users reasonable control. Driver updates are delivered through Windows Update, saving users the trouble of hunting for drivers themselves. In fact, many issues on long‑unupdated computers (random blue screens, inability to install new software, peripheral incompatibility, etc.) often disappear automatically after installing all Windows and driver updates. Therefore, keeping Windows Update enabled and checking it regularly is one of the simplest and most effective ways to maintain a healthy system.

title: FileManagement
content: Turn Off BitLocker Turn Off BitLocker Turn Off BitLocker The very first thing you do after getting a new laptop: turn off BitLocker. BitLocker is Windows's full‑disk encryption feature. It encrypts your drive, and only a recovery key can unlock it. That sounds secure, but for individual users, the downsides heavily outweigh any benefit: You will almost never need it. BitLocker is designed for corporate or government scenarios where a lost device might leak sensitive data. The chance of losing your personal laptop is tiny, and your data is not that valuable to an attacker. If your system crashes, the motherboard fails, or you lose the recovery key, all your data is gone forever. Microsoft will not help you decrypt it. It slightly reduces drive performance, especially for small file reads and writes. Your data is priceless. I strongly suggest you turn BitLocker off to avoid the risk of permanent data loss. How to check and disable it: Open Settings → Privacy & security → Device encryption (or search for "BitLocker"). If it says "Off", you are fine. If it says "On", open PowerShell or Command Prompt as Administrator and run: Wait for decryption to complete. You can check progress with in the same terminal. Decryption may take from a few tens of minutes to hours. You can use your computer normally during this time, but keep it plugged in and powered on until done. Ignore anyone who tells you to "keep BitLocker". For you, turning it off is the smarter choice. Appendix 3: File Management and Storage Philosophy This chapter covers only the most essential file management and storage operations. More in‑depth discussions are in the "Extended Reading" section. 3.1 Partition Your Drive: Separate C: and D: New computers usually come with a single C: drive. Putting everything (system, documents, downloads) on C: means that if the system crashes and you need to reinstall Windows, all your data is lost. So it is wise to split the drive into two partitions. Example: Your laptop has a 1TB SSD. You can leave 300GB for C: and use the remaining ~650GB for D:. C: drive (system): Only Windows, drivers, and a few programs that must be on C: (e.g., certain development tools). Nothing else. D: drive (data): Your documents, photos, videos, downloaded installers, Steam library, project code, etc. Why do this? If Windows breaks and you have to reinstall, you only need to format C:. Everything on D: remains untouched. After reinstalling Steam, you can add the D: Steam library folder in settings – no need to redownload games. How to do it: Use the built‑in Disk Management (right‑click "This PC" → Manage → Disk Management). Right‑click C: and choose "Shrink Volume" to free up space, then create a new simple volume with the free space and assign it drive letter D:. If unsure, search for "how to partition laptop drive" on YouTube and follow a recent tutorial. 3.2 Organise Files with Numbered Prefixes Do not just pile folders directly on D:. It is much better to use a category + number scheme. For example: 01Work: Internships, part‑time jobs, student club documents. 02Study: Course materials, papers, eBooks. 03Media: Personal photos, music, movies. 04Downloads: Browser cache. Clean it once a week or month – move useful files to other folders, delete the rest. 05_Archive: Things you no longer use but cannot bear to delete (e.g., old versions of your graduation project). Why the number prefix? Windows sorts by character order. appears before , so your most important folders are always the first you see when you open D:. 3.3 Game Storage: Delete When Done, Keep Cloud Saves Games on Steam and Epic are now huge (50–100GB). You usually play only two or three at a time. Games you have finished and will never touch again just waste space. My approach: Keep only the games you are actively playing. When you finish a game (or know you will not touch it for a while), first make sure your cloud saves are synchronised (Steam does this by default), then uninstall it from Steam. When you want to replay it, just download it again. 3.4 Backup Strategy: The 3‑2‑1 Rule (Simplified) The 3‑2‑1 rule is a basic consensus in data protection: 3 copies of your data (original + two backups) 2 different storage media (e.g., internal SSD + external hard drive) 1 off‑site copy (e.g., cloud storage) For students, you can simplify: Original data: On your laptop D: drive. Local backup: Every two weeks or every month, copy your most important folders (documents, photos, code projects) to an external hard drive. Off‑site backup: Use a cloud service like Baidu Netdisk, OneDrive, or Aliyun Drive to sync a copy of your important files. Never use a no‑name USB flash drive as your only backup! Cheap drives can die after just a few uses. If you need a flash drive, buy a reputable brand (e.g., SanDisk CZ74). For more details on hard drive selection and backup, see the Extended Reading section. 3.5 Simple Cloud Storage Choices If possible, prefer international services: OneDrive (the 1TB that comes with Office 365), Google Drive, Dropbox. Their clients are stable and they treat privacy somewhat better. Chinese alternatives: Baidu Netdisk (speed limited but usable for incremental backup), Aliyun Drive (currently less throttling). Highly sensitive data (e.g., ID card scans, password backups): Never upload them directly to any cloud. Use an open‑source encryption tool like VeraCrypt or a password‑protected AES‑256 7‑Zip archive, then upload the encrypted file. 3.6 Keep Your Computer Clock Accurate: Change the NTP Server If your computer clock is often wrong (e.g., a few minutes slow after boot), it is because Windows's default time server is overseas and has high latency. Manual sync steps: Right‑click the clock on the taskbar → "Adjust date/time". Under "Synchronise your clock", click "Sync now". If it fails, click "Add clocks for different time zones" → switch to the "Internet Time" tab → "Change settings". In the "Server" box, enter one of these: (Tencent Cloud) (Alibaba Cloud) Click "Update now". Wait a few seconds for success. If you are a university student, search for "your university name + ntp server" to get an on‑campus server (e.g., Tsinghua has ), which has even lower latency. After this, your clock will automatically stay accurate. Extended Reading The following sections contain more detailed technical discussions and advanced knowledge. Each is independent – you can read any of them without relying on the main text. Extended 1: When BitLocker Actually Makes Sense (You Don't Need It) BitLocker is only useful for the very few people who need extremely high security – handling trade secrets, legally sensitive information. If that is not you, ignore it. Just turn it off. Extended 2: A Closer Look at Partitioning When using Disk Management to partition: The C: drive on a new computer has lots of free space. The "Shrink Volume" option shows the maximum you can shrink. After shrinking, you see unallocated space. Right‑click it → "New Simple Volume", follow the wizard, assign D: as the drive letter, and choose NTFS file system. If you accidentally delete the system partition, do not panic. Search for "Windows installation media repair boot". Recommended video tutorial: Search for "how to partition laptop drive" on Bilibili or YouTube, pick a recent one with high views. Extended 3: Manually Backing Up Game Saves Although platforms like Steam offer cloud saves, some older games or pirated copies do not sync. Saves are usually located at: or (AppData is hidden; you can type the path directly into File Explorer's address bar) After finishing a game, consider manually copying its save folder to . Extended 4: Buying and Using Hard Disk Drives for Backup (In‑Depth) If you plan to buy a mechanical hard drive for cold backups (rarely powered on), here are some practical points. HDDs are sensitive to vibration while running. Do not move or bump them when powered on. CMR vs. SMR – My personal preference CMR (Conventional Magnetic Recording) offers stable random write performance and easier data recovery – even if a small part is damaged, the rest is usually still accessible. SMR (Shingled Magnetic Recording) overlaps tracks to increase density (about 25% more capacity than CMR at the same platter count), which lowers cost per gigabyte (typically 10‑20% cheaper). For purely sequential writes of cold data, SMR is technically fine. But personally, I simply dislike SMR. Its random write IOPS can drop by more than 50%, and localised damage may affect related tracks, making recovery trickier. So I only recommend CMR drives. Among consumer drives, Western Digital Red Pro and Seagate IronWolf Pro are typically CMR – search for "model number + CMR" before buying. Can SSDs be used for cold backups? Not recommended. SSDs store data as electrical charge, and over long periods without power (2‑3 years) the charge gradually leaks, causing data corruption. At higher temperatures, retention time drops further (about one year at 30°C, only half a year at 55°C). For important cold data, a mechanical hard drive is safer – but of course, always keep multiple copies everywhere. Using spare SSDs with an M.2 enclosure If you have a spare M.2 SSD, you can buy an M.2 enclosure to turn it into a fast portable drive. A brand I know with decent value is ITGZ (also called IGTZ). They offer an all‑metal enclosure with a 9210B controller, supporting 2230/2242/2280 drives, priced around 6‑10 USD. Note that the enclosure itself is cheap, but since SSD prices are currently high, buying a brand new SSD just for this purpose may not be cost‑effective. B Key vs. M Key – for those who happen to need it M.2 slots come in three key types: M Key: Supports PCIe x4 (high‑performance NVMe SSDs), notch on the right, bandwidth up to 32Gbps. B Key: Mainly supports SATA and PCIe x2, notch on the left, lower bandwidth. B+M Key: Both notches present, compatible with both slot types, but actual protocol depends on the slot. Regular power‑on – for all electronics Whether mechanical or solid‑state, leaving a drive without power for too long can cause issues. Mechanical drives need the spindle motor to spin occasionally for lubrication. For SSDs, JEDEC specifications state that data retention is measured under specific temperature conditions beyond which data may be lost. It is advisable to power on your backup drives every 3‑6 months, let them run for a few minutes, and check their health status. USB‑to‑SATA adapters and safe removal If you use a USB‑to‑SATA adapter (often called an "easy cable") with a 3.5‑inch mechanical drive, make sure it comes with a separate 12V power supply. USB power alone is often insufficient and may cause recognition failures or damage. When unplugging, always click the "Safely Remove Hardware" icon in the Windows system tray and wait for confirmation before unplugging. The safest method is simply shutting down the computer – on shutdown, the system will automatically park the heads. Never pull the USB cable while the drive activity light is still blinking; that can easily cause the heads to crash onto the platters, creating physical bad sectors. SATA connector insertion limit SATA connectors have a limited insertion cycle (typically around 50‑100 times). Do not plug and unplug just for fun. If you use a USB‑to‑SATA adapter board, you can leave the drive attached to the board and only unplug the USB cable – this spares the SATA connector. The same applies to USB‑to‑SATA cables: keep the whole assembly connected and avoid repeatedly disconnecting the SATA end. Cable recommendation When buying Type‑C cables for external drives or laptop charging, consider looking for Luxshare OEM cables. Luxshare is a key Apple supply chain manufacturer and a leader in high‑speed cables. On second‑hand markets (e.g., Xianyu), you can sometimes find Luxshare 240W PD 3.1 USB‑C cables for less than 3 USD. Their build quality and electrical performance far exceed no‑name cables at the same price, making them great for drive enclosures or laptop charging. Another channel called "Scientific Picking" may also offer good deals on factory‑surplus cables. Extended 5: Practical Cloud Encryption For sensitive files (ID scans, financial records, password backups), you must encrypt them before uploading. Method 1 – VeraCrypt Download VeraCrypt and create an encrypted volume (a virtual hard drive). Drag your sensitive files into it. After closing, you get a file. Upload that file to the cloud. To decrypt, you need VeraCrypt and the password. The cloud provider cannot read the contents. Method 2 – 7‑Zip encryption Right‑click the files/folder → 7‑Zip → Add to archive. Set a password, choose AES‑256 as the encryption method. Upload the resulting or file. Remember to also check "Encrypt file names" so that the contents are truly hidden. Extended 6: How NTP Time Synchronisation Works NTP (Network Time Protocol) is used to calibrate your computer's clock over the internet. The motherboard has a CMOS battery that keeps time when the PC is off, but the battery eventually dies (usually after 3‑5 years). If your computer resets to 1970 every time you boot, the CMOS battery is dead – replace it with a CR2032. Changing to a domestic NTP server greatly improves sync success rates. title: Ports
content: Appendix 4: Quick Reference for Common Ports This chapter helps you identify the shape, purpose, speed, and power delivery of various ports on your laptop – so you don‘t buy the wrong cables or docking stations. The Must-Read part covers only what you need day‑to‑day (does it fit? can it do the job?). Detailed version tables are in Extended Reading – consult them when you need specifics. First, understand the unit conversion Port speeds are often quoted in Mbps (megabits per second) or Gbps (gigabits per second), but file copy dialogs show MB/s (megabytes per second). The conversion is: 8 Mbps = 1 MB/s Examples: USB 2.0 theoretical speed: 480 Mbps → about 60 MB/s (slower in practice) Gigabit Ethernet: 1000 Mbps → 125 MB/s Just divide by 8 to get the theoretical MB/s (real‑world will be lower). 4.1 The Minimum You Need to Know For most ports, if the shape matches, it will work. Only a few cases require checking versions. USB: Black or white plastic inside means slow (USB 2.0, about 30‑40 MB/s actual). Blue plastic or "SS" logo means fast (USB 3.x, several hundred MB/s actual). Charging: Only Type‑C ports, with both your laptop and charger supporting PD (Power Delivery), can fast‑charge the laptop. Regular Type‑A ports cannot charge a laptop. External display: Both HDMI and Type‑C work. For 4K 60Hz or higher, prefer Type‑C or DisplayPort (DP). Ethernet and headphone jack: If the shape fits, plug it in. 4.2 USB Ports (Practical Guide) Shapes Type‑A (flat rectangle): Common on flash drives, mice. Blue plastic or "SS" logo means high speed. Type‑C (oval, reversible): The main port on new laptops. You cannot tell speed by shape alone – it could be slow USB 2.0 or very fast USB4. Check your laptop's specs. Type‑B (square / trapezoidal): Used on printers, scanners, some drive adapters. Insertion cycles are limited – keep it plugged in and only unplug the other end. Mini / Micro USB: Old devices, now obsolete. Power delivery (laptop charging) Only Type‑C with PD can charge your laptop. The port usually has a PD or lightning bolt logo next to it. Charger, cable, and laptop must all support the same or higher PD power level. Detailed USB version table (2.0 / 3.x / USB4) is in Extended Reading at the end of this appendix. 4.3 Display Ports HDMI (trapezoidal, flat): Connect to TVs, monitors, projectors. If your 4K monitor shows only 30Hz (choppy motion), the cable or port may be an old version. Use a cable labelled "HDMI 2.0" or higher. DP / Mini‑DP (rectangular or small rectangle): High bandwidth, good for high resolution and high refresh rates. Common on desktop monitors and some laptops. VGA (blue trapezoid, 15 pins): For old projectors. New laptops don't have it – you'll need an active HDMI‑to‑VGA adapter. Simple rule: For 4K 60Hz or higher, prefer Type‑C to DP or DP directly. HDMI can also do it, but check your hardware. 4.4 Network Port RJ45 (square with a clip): Wired Ethernet – stable and low latency. Thin‑and‑light laptops often omit it; use a Type‑C to RJ45 adapter. 4.5 Audio Port 3.5mm headphone jack (round): Almost all laptops keep this. Plug in headphones, mic, or headset. 4.6 Thunderbolt vs. USB4 Thunderbolt port: Type‑C shape with a ⚡ lightning bolt logo next to it. Without that logo, it‘s just regular USB. Do you need Thunderbolt? Only if you need to connect an external GPU or two 4K displays simultaneously. For daily office work, one monitor, or ordinary storage, regular USB 3.x or USB4 is enough. Detailed Thunderbolt vs. USB4 comparison table (bandwidth, power, daisy‑chaining) is in Extended Reading. 4.7 One‑Cable Display with Reverse Charging "One‑cable connection": a single Type‑C cable between laptop and monitor that carries video, charges the laptop, and extends USB ports. Requirements: Monitor supports PD output (at least 65W) Laptop supports PD charging Cable supports 5A current (100W or higher) No side effects – your laptop‘s power management handles it safely. 4.8 TGX Port (Specific Laptop Models) Looks like a slim Type‑C, labelled TGX. Only found on a few Lenovo ThinkBook models (14+/16+). Used to connect an external desktop graphics card. Regular users can completely ignore this. 4.9 Cable Advice A poor‑quality cable will cripple your expensive devices. Common problems: slow charging, 4K display blackout or flickering, device not recognised. Recommendation: Luxshare's 240W USB4 universal cable – supports PD 3.1 240W charging, USB4 40Gbps data, and 8K video. 4.10 Memory Cards (SD / microSD) Laptop card slots come in two shapes: SD card (full‑size, about the size of a postage stamp) microSD / TF card (tiny, used in phones and drones) Speed rating simplified Photos or normal video: buy a card labelled C10 (10 inside a circle) or U1. 4K video recording: buy a card labelled U3 or V30. Ignore other letters (A1/A2, V60/V90) unless you know you need them. Physical interface type Most thin‑and‑light laptops have UHS‑I slots (one row of gold contacts) – theoretical maximum about 100 MB/s. A few high‑end models have UHS‑II (two rows of contacts) – can do >300 MB/s. To tell: flip the card over and count the contact rows. Check your laptop‘s manual for what it supports. CFexpress (for professional cameras) Regular users can ignore this completely. If you own a high‑end camera and need very fast continuous shooting or high‑bitrate video, check your camera's manual for the correct CFexpress type (A, B, or C) before buying a card. 4.11 SATA Port SATA (Serial Advanced Technology Attachment) is an older interface standard for connecting hard drives. New laptops no longer include SATA ports, but you may encounter external drive enclosures, desktop hard drives, or drives pulled from old laptops. Shape and versions A SATA connection has two parts: Data connector (L‑shaped, 7 pins): short flat connector, carries data. Power connector (longer, 15 pins): supplies power. Common SATA versions: SATA 3.0: mainstream, speed 6 Gbps (about 550‑560 MB/s actual). SATA 2.0: 3 Gbps, older devices. All versions have identical physical connectors and are backwards compatible. Usage 2.5‑inch drives (laptop HDDs, older SSDs): use SATA data + power. 3.5‑inch desktop drives: also SATA, but require 12V power (2.5‑inch drives need only 5V). Therefore, external 3.5‑inch drives need a separate power supply. Optical drives (obsolete): also use SATA. Using an external SATA drive (USB‑to‑SATA adapter / enclosure) If you have a spare SATA drive and want to use it as an external drive: Buy a USB‑to‑SATA adapter cable (often called "easy cable") or a drive enclosure. Watch the power: 2.5‑inch drives can run on USB power (5V). 3.5‑inch drives must use an adapter with a separate 12V power supply; otherwise they won‘t spin up. Safe removal: Always use "Safely Remove Hardware" in the Windows system tray, or shut down the computer before unplugging. Never unplug while the drive is reading or writing – this can damage the heads or create bad sectors. Insertion cycle limit SATA connectors have a limited mating life (about 50‑100 cycles). If you frequently connect an external SATA drive, leave the SATA side of the adapter or enclosure permanently attached to the drive, and only unplug the USB side. This preserves the SATA connector. Extended Reading (Technical Details) The following sections contain detailed tables and advanced knowledge. Read them when you need specifics. Extended 1: USB Version Full Table | USB Version | Alias | Max Speed | Theoretical Bandwidth (approx) | Common Use | |-------------|-------|-----------|-------------------------------|-------------| | USB 2.0 | Hi‑Speed | 480 Mbps | 60 MB/s | Keyboards, mice, old flash drives | | USB 3.0 / 3.1 Gen1 | USB 3.0 | 5 Gbps | 500 MB/s | Normal flash drives, external HDDs | | USB 3.1 Gen2 | USB 3.1 | 10 Gbps | 1.2 GB/s | Fast external SSDs | | USB 3.2 Gen2x2 | USB 3.2 | 20 Gbps | 2.4 GB/s | High‑end external SSDs | | USB4 | USB4 | 40 Gbps | 4 GB/s | Laptops, docks, displays | Identification: USB 2.0 ports usually have black or white plastic inside. USB 3.x ports typically have blue plastic or logos like "SS" (SuperSpeed) or "10" (10Gbps). Type‑C ports cannot be identified by appearance alone. Extended 2: HDMI Version Quick Table | HDMI Version | Max Resolution / Refresh | Bandwidth | Notes | |--------------|--------------------------|-----------|-------| | 1.4 | 4K 30Hz | 10.2 Gbps | Legacy | | 2.0 | 4K 60Hz | 18 Gbps | Mainstream | | 2.1 TMDS | 4K 60Hz | 18 Gbps | Essentially renamed 2.0 | | 2.1 FRL | 4K 120Hz / 8K 60Hz | 48 Gbps | True 2.1 | When buying an HDMI cable, look for "HDMI 2.1 certified" and explicit support for 4K 120Hz or 8K. Extended 3: Thunderbolt vs. USB4 Comparison | Feature | Thunderbolt 3 | Thunderbolt 4 | Thunderbolt 5 | USB4 (baseline) | |---------|---------------|---------------|---------------|------------------| | Theoretical bandwidth | 40 Gbps | 40 Gbps | 80 Gbps (120/40 symmetric mode) | 40 Gbps (optional) | | Minimum PCIe bandwidth | 16 Gbps | mandatory 32 Gbps | 64 Gbps | not guaranteed | | Minimum video output | 1x 4K | mandatory 2x 4K | 2x 6K / 3x 4K | not guaranteed | | Minimum port power | 9W | mandatory 15W | 15W+ | only 7.5W | | Daisy‑chaining | supported | supported | supported | not guaranteed | | Certification | Intel | Intel | Intel | none | Conclusion: USB4 baseline is loose – vendors can make cut‑down versions (20Gbps, low power). Thunderbolt 4/5 enforce higher minimums. A Type‑C port without a lightning bolt logo is just regular USB. Extended 4: Memory Card Speed Class Full Table | Logo | Name | Minimum Write Speed | |------|------|---------------------| | C2/C4/C6/C10 | Speed Class | 2/4/6/10 MB/s | | U1 / U3 | UHS Speed Class | 10 / 30 MB/s | | V10–V90 | Video Speed Class | 10–90 MB/s | | A1 / A2 | Application Performance Class | random IOPS | A card may show C10, U3, V30, A2 together – it meets all those minimums. Extended 5: SD Express and CFexpress SD Express: Brings PCIe bus to SD cards. Theoretical speed up to 985 MB/s (PCIe 3.0 x1) or 4 GB/s (PCIe 4.0 x2). However, as of 2026, very few laptops support it – ordinary users do not need it. CFexpress: For professional cameras, based on PCIe/NVMe. Three physically incompatible types: Type A (~2 GB/s), Type B (~4 GB/s), Type C (~8 GB/s). Always check your camera's manual before buying. Extended 6: SATA Versions and AHCI SATA 3.0 has a theoretical speed of 6 Gbps, but due to 8b/10b encoding (each 10 bits transmitted contain 8 bits of real data), the effective bandwidth is about 4.8 Gbps, or roughly 560 MB/s. This is the ceiling for SATA – even the fastest SSD cannot exceed this speed when connected via SATA. AHCI (Advanced Host Controller Interface) is the driver protocol for SATA drives. It was designed for mechanical hard drives and is not well optimised for the high queue depth and parallelism of SSDs. In contrast, NVMe (used by M.2 drives) fully unlocks SSD performance. This is why M.2 NVMe drives are much faster than SATA SSDs. If you use a USB‑to‑SATA adapter, Windows will handle AHCI automatically – you don‘t need to worry about it.

title: Browsers
content: Appendix 5: Web Browsers This appendix covers basic browser usage, search techniques, how to ask questions effectively, and commonly used extensions. 5.1 Which Browser to Choose Windows comes with Microsoft Edge, which is built on Chromium and offers good compatibility. You can use it as is. Firefox is also a solid choice. Please avoid any Chinese-branded browsers such as 360 Extreme Browser or 2345 Browser. 5.2 Multi‑Threaded Downloading: FDM The built‑in downloader in browsers is single‑threaded. Large files download slowly, and if the connection drops, you may have to restart from scratch. Multi‑threaded tools split a file into chunks and download them simultaneously, which is faster and supports resuming interrupted downloads. FDM (Free Download Manager) is recommended. It is free, open‑source, and ad‑free. During installation, enable the browser integration plugin. No manual configuration is needed. When you download a large file (several hundred MB or more), FDM will be invoked automatically. FDM Download Link 5.3 Search Engines Bing is recommended. It is accessible from within China and shows fewer ads than Baidu. If you have access to Google, its English search results are more accurate. 5.4 Effective Search Tips Do not type full sentences. Extract and use only the core keywords. Examples: Bad: Better: Useful search operators: | Operator | Purpose | Example | |----------|---------|---------| | | Restrict to a specific website | | | | Restrict to a file format | | | | Exact phrase match | | | minus sign | Exclude a word | | When searching for an error message, copy the complete error code (e.g., ) rather than describing what happened – it works much better. 5.5 Judging Whether Information Is True or False Check the source: Prioritize official sources and reputable media. Be cautious with unknown self‑media accounts. Check the date: Outdated information may no longer be valid. Cross‑validate: Compare different sources. Look at comments: If many commenters disagree or point out factual errors, the content is likely unreliable. Watch for clickbait headlines: Words like “shocking,” “urgent,” “watch before deletion” often signal hype or misinformation. For academic purposes, use Google Scholar or your university library’s databases. The references in English Wikipedia articles can serve as a starting point. 5.6 How to Ask Questions and Netiquette When asking for help, include as much of the following as possible: The full error message (text or screenshot) Your environment: OS version, software version, hardware model, etc. Log files: Many programs and games generate files in their installation folder or under . Copy the last few dozen lines. Example (game crashing to desktop): Problem: Game goes black and crashes on startup Environment: Windows 11 22H2, graphics driver 610.47, game version 1.2.3 Error message: Last lines of the log: [paste here] Already tried: Updated drivers, verified game file integrity Basic netiquette: Try to find the answer yourself first. If you can’t, then ask. Describe the problem clearly and mention what you have already tried. After receiving help, report back the outcome so others can learn. Do not send private messages for public questions – ask in public forums/channels. 5.7 Useful Browser Extensions Extensions should be installed from the official stores (Edge Add‑ons, Chrome Web Store, Firefox Add‑ons). 5.7.1 Ad Blocking: uBlock Origin Open‑source, lightweight, and blocks most ads and trackers. For small websites or personal blogs that you visit often, if the ads are not intrusive, you can disable uBlock (click the extension icon → the power icon turns gray) or add the site to the allowlist. Those sites rely on ad revenue to stay running. 5.7.2 Cat Catch Sniffs out the real addresses of audio and video on a page and lets you download them. When a page has media playing, the extension icon shows a number; click it and choose what to download. Useful for recording online lectures, background music, etc. 5.7.3 LeechBlock NG Limits the time you can spend on certain websites. You can set a maximum daily allowance or specific allowed time windows. Once the limit is reached, access is automatically blocked. Helps control time spent on social media or video sites. 5.7.4 Tampermonkey A user‑script manager. You can install scripts from GreasyFork (greasyfork.org) to auto‑fill forms, remove ads, and add custom functionality. Security reminders: Do not install scripts from unknown sources, especially those promising “free VIP” or “shopping bot”. Before installing, look at the script code. If it requests many external permissions (e.g., ), do not install it. Do not install extensions from outside the official stores, especially “free VPN” or “web accelerator” tools. Extended Reading The following sections go into browser internals and technical details. They are more advanced. It is recommended to skim them first – just be aware these concepts exist. When you run into a specific problem later, you can search again using the keywords you learned here. If something puzzles you or you want to dive deeper, I suggest looking up MDN and W3Schools. Extended 1: Browser Engine The browser engine (rendering engine) turns HTML, CSS, and JavaScript code into a visible page. Blink: Used by Chrome, Edge, Opera, Brave, and others. Currently the highest market share. Gecko: Used by Firefox, completely open‑source. WebKit: Used by Safari. Blink originally forked from WebKit. Ordinary users do not need to worry about these differences. Very rarely, an old website may say “Please use Chrome” – but Edge will actually work fine too. If a site looks broken, try switching browsers. Extended 2: Web Page Structure (HTML, CSS, JavaScript) A web page is built from three languages: HTML: Defines content and structure. The browser parses it into a DOM tree. CSS: Defines style and layout – colors, fonts, positioning, etc. JavaScript: Defines interactive behavior – button clicks, carousels, form validation, etc. TypeScript: A superset of JavaScript that adds type annotations. It needs to be compiled into JavaScript to run. ES6: The 2015 version of JavaScript, introducing arrow functions, classes, modules, etc. All modern browsers support it. Responsive design: Uses CSS media queries ( ) to automatically adapt to different screen widths. Press F12 → click the device simulation icon (a small phone) to see how a site looks on mobile. Progressive enhancement: Start with basic content (plain HTML) accessible on all devices, then add styles and interactions on top. This works better for older devices and users with disabilities. Extended 3: Response Headers and Status Codes When a browser requests a page, the server returns response headers. Press F12 → Network tab → click any request to see them. Common status codes: 200: Success 301: Permanent redirect 302 (or 307): Temporary redirect 403: Forbidden 404: Page not found 500: Internal server error Extended 4: User‑Agent (UA) A string the browser sends to the server, containing browser name, version, and operating system. The server can use the UA to return different versions (e.g., mobile site vs. desktop site). Press F12 → device simulation (choose a phone model), then refresh the page – you are now pretending to be a mobile device. You can also install a UA switcher extension. Do not use UA spoofing to scrape website data; always follow the rules. Extended 5: Cookie, localStorage, IndexedDB Three ways browsers store data locally: | Name | Capacity | Lifetime | Sent with requests | Main use | |------|----------|----------|--------------------|-----------| | Cookie | 4KB | Can set expiration | Yes | Login state, user tracking | | localStorage | 5–10MB | Permanent (unless manually cleared) | No | User preferences, theme settings | | IndexedDB | Hundreds of MB | Permanent | No | Offline cache for large structured data | Cookie: Stores a session ID. If you clear cookies, you will be logged out. localStorage: Simple API, good for small settings. IndexedDB: Supports indexes and transactions, but the API is more complex. Many PWAs use it to cache data. View and manage: F12 → Application → Storage section. Extended 6: Chrome/Edge Flags and Firefox about:config Entry points for experimental browser features: Chrome/Edge: Type or in the address bar. Firefox: Type in the address bar, then click “Accept the Risk”. If changes cause problems, click “Reset all” to restore defaults. Extended 7: Main Panels of Developer Tools (F12) Elements: View and edit HTML/CSS (temporary, local only). Console: Shows JavaScript errors and warnings; you can also execute JS code. Sources: View source files and set breakpoints to debug JS. Network: Records all network requests – status codes, timings, request/response data. Application: Manage cookies, localStorage, IndexedDB, and Service Workers. Performance: Record performance data to analyze lag or jank. Lighthouse: Provides a comprehensive score for performance, accessibility, SEO, etc. Extended 8: Service Worker and PWA Service Worker: A script that runs in the background of the browser. It can intercept network requests, manage caches, and send push notifications – even when the page is not open. PWA (Progressive Web App): Uses Service Workers and other technologies to give a web app a native‑like experience – it can be installed on the desktop, work offline, and receive push notifications. When you see an install icon (a computer screen with a down arrow) in the Chrome or Edge address bar, you can click it to install the site as a desktop app. Extended 9: CORS (Cross‑Origin Resource Sharing) The browser’s security policy, the “same‑origin policy”, prevents a web page from making requests to a different domain. If a page legitimately needs to request data from another domain, that target server must include the header in its response. When developing local web pages, you often run into CORS errors. To fix them, either configure the backend to send the proper headers or use a proxy. Understanding CORS helps you understand why certain API calls from a web page might fail. Extended 10: WebFonts, Browser Cache, and WebAssembly (Wasm) WebFonts Fonts used on websites (e.g., Noto Sans, Source Han Sans) are often not installed on the operating system, so they must be downloaded from the server. These font files ( , , ) are called WebFonts. A website declares which font files to download using the rule in CSS. The browser downloads them and caches them locally, so they don’t need to be downloaded again on subsequent visits. Common formats: WOFF2 (high compression, used by modern browsers), WOFF (for older browser compatibility), TTF (uncompressed, rarely used). If text on a site flickers or appears as squares (gibberish), WebFonts might have failed to load. Press F12 → Network tab → filter by “Font” to see if font requests return 404. Browser Cache The HTTP cache stores downloaded resources (images, CSS, JS, fonts, etc.) on the local disk. When you revisit the same page, resources are read from the local disk instead of being requested from the server again, which speeds up loading significantly. Cache mechanism in a nutshell: When a server returns a resource, it includes headers like or that tell the browser how long it may cache the resource. For example, means the resource is valid for 24 hours; the browser will use the cached copy without even asking the server during that time. After the cache expires, the browser sends a “conditional request” using or to ask the server whether the resource has changed. If it hasn’t, the server returns and the browser continues using the cached copy. Manually controlling the cache: Press to force a refresh that re‑downloads everything from the server. Press F12 → Network tab → check “Disable cache” to force fresh downloads during debugging. Clear the browser cache: Settings → Privacy and security → Clear browsing data → choose “Cached images and files”. WebAssembly (Wasm) WebAssembly is a binary instruction format that runs in the browser. Its goal is near‑native execution speed while maintaining safety. Languages like C, C++, Rust, and Go can be compiled into Wasm and then called from JavaScript inside a web page. Why do we need Wasm? Traditional JavaScript is interpreted (though modern JS engines use JIT compilation), but for computationally intensive tasks (video encoding/decoding, image processing, game physics, cryptography) it may still not be fast enough. Wasm offers a lower‑level, pre‑compiled format that executes significantly faster. A simple Wasm example Here’s how to write a C function that adds two numbers, compile it to Wasm, and call it from HTML. Step 1: Write C code ( ) Step 2: Compile to Wasm After installing the Emscripten toolchain, run: This generates an file. Step 3: Load and call it from HTML Real‑world use cases: Figma: The graphics rendering engine is implemented in Wasm. AutoCAD Web: The browser version of the CAD software. Video / image processing: For example, ffmpeg compiled to Wasm enables online transcoding. Game engines: Unity and Unreal Engine can export to Wasm for web deployment. Ordinary users do not need to interact with Wasm directly. But knowing about it helps you understand why certain web apps run so fast and why your CPU usage might suddenly spike – the page could be running a heavy Wasm computation task.

title: Proxy
content: Appendix 6: Proxy This appendix explains the differences between proxy, VPN, and related concepts, as well as how to use common proxy tools. No specific service providers are recommended. 6.1 Relationship Between Concepts Proxy: An intermediary network service. Your device sends requests to a proxy server, which accesses the target website on your behalf and returns the result. Proxies can bypass network restrictions, but they usually only work for specific applications (e.g., browsers). VPN (Virtual Private Network) : Creates an encrypted tunnel between your device and the target server. All network traffic (including system background traffic, UDP, etc.) goes through the tunnel. VPNs operate at the network layer and affect the entire system. Ladder: A colloquial term for circumvention tools, including both proxies and VPN services. Airport: Slang for a commercial proxy service provider – literally “the place where you get a ladder”. Users purchase a plan and receive a subscription link, which they import into a client. To put it simply: proxy and VPN are technical implementations, while “ladder” and “airport” are community slang. 6.2 Clash and Its Variants Clash is a rule‑based proxy core that supports multiple protocols (HTTP, SOCKS5, Shadowsocks, VMess, etc.). It has no graphical interface on its own and needs a GUI front‑end. Main variants: | Name | Description | |------|-------------| | Clash (original) | The earliest core, now unmaintained. | | Clash Premium | A closed‑source version by the original author, added features like TUN mode, also discontinued. | | Clash Meta (mihomo) | An active fork maintained by the open‑source community, with more features and the most commonly used today. It is described separately later. | | Clash Verge Rev | A cross‑platform GUI front‑end (Windows/macOS/Linux) based on the Clash Meta core. Clean interface, suitable for daily use. | | Clash for Windows (CFW) | Once the most popular Windows GUI, now discontinued and no longer recommended. | | ClashX / ClashX Pro | GUI front‑ends for macOS. | | ClashMetaForAndroid (CMFA) | Android GUI based on the mihomo core. | For ordinary users, simply use Clash Verge (desktop) and ClashMetaForAndroid (Android). 6.3 YAML Configuration Files The core of Clash is a configuration file (usually ) written in YAML format. The subscription link you get from an airport is essentially this file. Basic structure of a configuration file: How to use: Obtain a subscription link (usually ) or download a file directly from your airport. In Clash Verge, click “Import” → “Import from URL” and paste the link; or manually place the config file into the config directory. Select a proxy group (e.g., choose a node in “PROXY”), then enable “System Proxy” or “TUN Mode”. Key fields: : List of nodes, each with type, address, port, encryption, etc. : Policy groups. means manual selection; automatically picks the fastest; switches in order. : Matching rules. They are evaluated from top to bottom; the first match applies. matches domain suffixes, matches IP ranges, matches geographic location, and is the catch‑all rule. 6.4 Shadowrocket Shadowrocket is a proxy client for iOS, supporting protocols such as SSR, VMess, Trojan, and also subscriptions. How to use: Purchase from the App Store (requires a US region account), about $2.99. Open the app, tap the “+” in the top‑right corner → choose “Subscribe”. Paste the subscription link provided by your airport and save. Go back to the home screen and tap the switch to connect. The first time you do this, you will be prompted to add a VPN configuration – allow it. You can adjust routing rules via “Configuration” → “Rules”. 6.5 Mihomo Mihomo (formerly Clash Meta) is the core maintained by the Clash open‑source community and is the foundation of all active Clash clients today. It fixes many issues from the original Clash and adds new protocols (such as WireGuard, Hysteria) and new features. Mihomo itself is a command‑line program; you do not need to run it separately. GUIs like Clash Verge and ClashMetaForAndroid all bundle the mihomo core. If you need to run it manually, download the binary for your platform from GitHub and start it with: 6.6 System Proxy Mode vs. TUN Mode Clash provides two ways to route traffic through the proxy. System Proxy Mode: Configures an HTTP/SOCKS5 proxy address in your system network settings (usually ). Only programs that “respect the system proxy” will go through the proxy. Most browsers and some applications do; but games, command‑line tools, and UDP traffic (e.g., DNS, voice chat) usually do not. Pros: Lightweight, good compatibility. Cons: Many types of traffic bypass the proxy. TUN Mode: Creates a virtual network interface. The operating system routes all traffic (TCP, UDP, ICMP) to this interface, where Clash processes it and forwards accordingly. Essentially a global proxy that works without any program having to cooperate. Games, Spotify clients, and system DNS will all go through the proxy. How to enable: In Clash Verge, go to “Settings” → install the TUN service (requires administrator privileges) → turn on the TUN Mode switch. Cons: Slightly higher resource usage than system proxy; may affect local network access (you may need to configure rules to allow LAN traffic). In general, use system proxy if you only browse the web. If you play games or use software that does not respect the system proxy, enable TUN Mode. 6.7 Shizuku Mode on Android Shizuku is an Android tool that allows ordinary apps to execute system‑level commands via ADB or root privileges, granting high permissions without root. In ClashMetaForAndroid (CMFA) , enabling TUN Mode normally requires root or Shizuku. Shizuku mode lets CMFA use TUN on non‑rooted phones. How to use: Install the Shizuku app (from GitHub or CoolAPK). Activate Shizuku as instructed (needs ADB or root): Connect to a computer and run Or activate via wireless debugging (Android 11+). Open CMFA → Settings → TUN Settings → choose “Shizuku Mode”. After granting permissions, TUN Mode will work normally. If your phone is already rooted, you can directly select “Root Mode” and skip Shizuku. Extended Reading The following sections cover proxy protocols and underlying mechanisms. They are more advanced. It is recommended to skim them first – just be aware these concepts exist. When you run into a specific problem later, you can search again using the keywords you learned here. Extended 1: Common Proxy Protocols HTTP Proxy: Only proxies HTTP traffic, transmits in plain text without encryption. Rarely used alone today. SOCKS5 Proxy: Proxies TCP and UDP traffic, does not inspect content, can be used with other encryption protocols. Clash’s mixed port offers both HTTP and SOCKS5. Shadowsocks (SS) : Encrypted SOCKS5 proxy, lightweight, weak obfuscation; already recognized by some ISPs. ShadowsocksR (SSR) : A derivative of SS with added obfuscation plugins, now gradually obsolete. VMess: The core protocol of V2Ray, strong encryption, supports dynamic ports. Trojan: Mimics HTTPS traffic, good camouflage. Hysteria: A QUIC (UDP)‑based protocol designed for aggressive speed boosting, works well on high‑packet‑loss networks. WireGuard: A next‑generation VPN protocol with kernel‑level implementation, now also supported by Mihomo. Extended 2: Detailed Clash Rule Types : Exact full domain name match. : Matches domain suffix, e.g., matches and . : Matches a keyword appearing in the domain name. : Matches IPv4 address ranges. : Matches IPv6 address ranges. : Uses the MaxMind database to determine the country of an IP address. (TUN mode only): Matches by process name. : Matches by source IP address (used for sharing proxy on a LAN). : Catch‑all rule; must be placed last. Extended 3: Virtual Network Interface Principle of TUN Mode TUN mode creates a virtual layer‑3 network interface (e.g., ) inside the operating system. The Clash core reads raw IP packets from this interface, parses the destination address, and decides – based on rules – whether to forward the request through a proxy or directly. For requests that need to go through a proxy, Clash encapsulates the original packet into a proxy protocol (e.g., Shadowsocks) and sends it to the remote server. The remote server decapsulates it, accesses the target, and sends back the response, which is then re‑encapsulated and returned. Because TUN mode requires full decapsulation and re‑encapsulation of packets, its CPU consumption is slightly higher than system proxy mode. Extended 4: IPv6 and Proxies Many airport nodes do not support IPv6. If your device has a public IPv6 address and you visit an IPv6 website, improper rule configuration may either cause the traffic to go direct (accessible) or go through a proxy (which might fail if the node doesn’t support IPv6). It is recommended to set in your configuration file, or explicitly handle IPv6 ranges with rules. Extended 5: DNS Split Routing Clash supports split DNS routing, meaning it uses different DNS servers depending on the domain name. A typical configuration: Domestic domains go to a domestic DNS (e.g., 114.114.114.114), returning domestic CDN addresses. Blocked domains go to the proxy node’s own DNS (or a trusted DNS such as 1.1.1.1) to avoid DNS poisoning. can detect whether a DNS result points to a foreign IP, providing further protection against poisoning.
